master_aspect_list.aspect: Presidio-backed PII entity detection and redaction
master_aspect_list.notes: Microsoft Presidio (analyzer + anonymizer, spaCy/DeBERTa NLP engine) is the single most reused PII engine across the set, wrapped four different ways.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Email address detection (regex)
master_aspect_list.notes: Cheapest and most universally implemented PII check; deterministic and effectively free to run at request time.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Phone number detection (regex, US and international)
master_aspect_list.notes: Widely present but formats vary by repo, so a single canonical pattern set should be standardised for AFNI.

master_aspect_list.aspect: US Social Security Number detection
master_aspect_list.notes: agentic_security-main is the only one excluding invalid 000/666/9xx area codes, which meaningfully cuts false positives.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Credit card detection with Luhn checksum validation
master_aspect_list.notes: Luhn validation is the difference between a usable check and a noisy one; hai-guardrails-main and safe-zone-main omit it and self-document false positives.

master_aspect_list.aspect: IBAN / bank account / routing number detection
master_aspect_list.notes: Financial identifiers are covered but country coverage is uneven and mostly EU/TR/US.

master_aspect_list.aspect: National / government ID detection across jurisdictions
master_aspect_list.notes: Infosys covers roughly 30 entity types including IN_PAN/IN_AADHAAR, UK_NHS, SG_NRIC, IT and AU IDs; safe-zone-main is Turkey-heavy; openguardrails-main only defines the vocabulary.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Healthcare PHI entities (ICD-10, MRN, NPI, DEA, medical licence)
master_aspect_list.notes: hai-guardrails-main has the most concrete healthcare regex table and is worth porting into Presidio as custom recognisers.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Network identifiers treated as PII (IP address, MAC, UUID)
master_aspect_list.notes: Useful for internal-infrastructure leakage, but noisy unless scoped to outbound responses only.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Zero-shot / NER-model PII detection beyond a fixed taxonomy
master_aspect_list.notes: NeMo's GLiNER-PII rail and LLM Guard's ai4privacy DeBERTa NER catch entity types no regex list anticipated.

master_aspect_list.aspect: LLM-as-judge PII leakage detection
master_aspect_list.notes: Good recall on unusual or partially redacted identifiers, but every call costs money and latency, so it belongs in evaluation rather than the hot path.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Reversible anonymisation with a vault for later re-identification
master_aspect_list.notes: The Anonymize/Deanonymize vault pair is unique in the set and is what makes redaction usable in real workflows rather than destructive.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Synthetic-value substitution, encryption and differential privacy
master_aspect_list.notes: Faker-based masking plus an encryption utility and a differential-privacy path; only repo offering non-destructive alternatives to plain redaction at this depth.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Multi-format and multi-modal PII scanning (PDF, Office, images/OCR, DICOM, video)
master_aspect_list.notes: Unique capability in the set and directly relevant if AFNI ingests client documents.

master_aspect_list.aspect: PII leakage red-team probing (ProPILE twin/triplet/quadruplet patterns)
master_aspect_list.notes: The offline counterpart to runtime PII filtering: it proves whether the model itself will surrender personal data under pressure.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Training-data memorisation / verbatim replay leak testing
master_aspect_list.notes: Detects a model reproducing memorised copyrighted or personal source text, using cloze prompts and MinHash near-duplicate matching.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Log and telemetry secret redaction before persistence
master_aspect_list.notes: Often forgotten: the guardrail log itself becomes a data-leak surface unless keys and tokens are scrubbed on the way in.

master_aspect_list.aspect: System-prompt and configuration leakage detection
master_aspect_list.notes: Covers both the runtime guard (leakage guard, canary token) and the attack probes (sysprompt_extraction, prompt-leakage vulnerability).

master_aspect_list.aspect: Standardised PII entity vocabulary and severity taxonomy
master_aspect_list.notes: Fourteen semantic PII buckets with country refinement plus an explicit Presidio-to-taxonomy mapping table, so different detectors can report in one language.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Fine-tuned transformer prompt-injection classifier
master_aspect_list.notes: LLM Guard's DeBERTa-v3 injection classifier (0.92 default threshold) is the strongest local, no-API-cost injection detector in the set.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Heuristic / fuzzy keyword prompt-injection screening
master_aspect_list.notes: Rebuff generates roughly 7,700 templated injection phrases and fuzzy-matches them; English-only but effectively free and a good first-pass filter.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Regex / phrase-list prompt-injection and jailbreak detection
master_aspect_list.notes: PyRIT's maintainers openly document their static injection scorer as high-recall and high-false-positive, which is the right way to use this layer.

master_aspect_list.aspect: LLM-as-judge prompt-injection scoring
master_aspect_list.notes: Catches novel phrasings the keyword tiers miss, at the cost of one model call per request.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Managed cloud jailbreak / prompt-shield API integration
master_aspect_list.notes: Azure Prompt Shields, AWS Bedrock Guardrails and Azure Content Safety are all already wired up as callable checks in these repos.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Vector-similarity lookup against a learned attack corpus
master_aspect_list.notes: Infosys ships a 1.7MB pre-computed jailbreak embedding bank; Rebuff grows its own corpus from confirmed leaks.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Canary-token insertion and leak detection
master_aspect_list.notes: A cheap, deterministic tripwire that proves context exfiltration actually happened rather than guessing at it.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Perplexity-based jailbreak heuristics (length ratio, prefix/suffix)
master_aspect_list.notes: NeMo publishes honest numbers: about 31% detection at 7.4% false positives for the length heuristic, but 49 of 50 GCG suffix attacks caught at 0.04% false positives.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Model-based jailbreak classifier on embeddings
master_aspect_list.notes: Random-forest over Snowflake arctic-embed embeddings (NeMo) or a fine-tuned DistilBERT (Infosys); both run locally without a paid API.

master_aspect_list.aspect: DAN / roleplay persona jailbreak attack library
master_aspect_list.notes: garak-main has the deepest catalogue (20-plus DAN variants plus an in-the-wild corpus) with a verified 127-prompt ablation set.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Encoding and obfuscation attacks (base64, ROT13, leetspeak, morse, unicode tags, ASCII art, steganography)
master_aspect_list.notes: The single most duplicated attack family; garak-main (20 encodings) and PyRIT-main (about 80 converters) are the definitive implementations.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Multi-turn iterative jailbreaks (Crescendo, TAP, PAIR, GOAT, Tree, Linear, ActorAttack)
master_aspect_list.notes: This is where real-world breaches happen and where single-turn filters fail; PyRIT-main has the most rigorous implementations with backtracking.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Many-shot / context-stuffing jailbreak simulation
master_aspect_list.notes: Directly exercises long-context models, and is the attack NeMo's context-bloat rail is designed to stop.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Optimisation-based adversarial suffix attacks (GCG, genetic, Best-of-N)
master_aspect_list.notes: Mostly shipped as fixed pre-computed suffixes rather than live gradient search, and maintainers note they are English-tuned.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Seed-template mutation with bandit-based success reuse
master_aspect_list.notes: JCB's WordNet synonym mutator plus UCB/epsilon-greedy seed selection is an efficient way to find cheap wins, but the code is research-grade.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Indirect / latent prompt injection via documents, RAG chunks and web content
master_aspect_list.notes: The highest-risk category for AFNI's RAG applications because the attacker never touches the chat box.

master_aspect_list.aspect: YARA-rule injection detection (SQLi, Jinja template, code, XSS)
master_aspect_list.notes: Fully local, deterministic and fast; note the sanitise action is unimplemented so only reject/omit are usable.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Insecure-output-handling scorers (SQLi, XSS, SSRF, SSTI, XXE, path traversal, LDAP, shell)
master_aspect_list.notes: PyRIT's nine regex scorers map explicitly to OWASP LLM02 and run with zero model calls, making them ideal runtime output rails.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Secrets and credential leak regex scanning
master_aspect_list.notes: garak-main carries 58 named provider patterns and llm-guard-main delegates to the maintained bc-detect-secrets plugin set.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Shannon-entropy gating to suppress secret false positives
master_aspect_list.notes: A small idea with a large payoff: every secret regex should be paired with an entropy floor before it blocks traffic.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Access-control red-teaming (BOLA, BFLA, RBAC bypass, debug access)
master_aspect_list.notes: Essential once an AI app can call authenticated internal APIs; note many promptfoo variants are remote-only plugins.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Agentic attack surface probes (goal theft, tool-metadata poisoning, orchestration abuse, agent identity abuse)
master_aspect_list.notes: DeepTeam's 12 agentic families with 19 matching judges is the deepest agent-specific coverage in the set.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Tool-call and tool-result schema validation (fail-closed, no model call)
master_aspect_list.notes: NeMo's IORails validate emitted tool calls against declared JSON schemas; DeepEval's ToolPermission enforces an allow/deny list deterministically.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Invisible-text, zero-width and ASCII-smuggling detection
master_aspect_list.notes: Deterministic, near-zero-cost and catches a whole class of filter-bypass tricks; should be non-negotiable in the input rail.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Context-bloat and prompt-stuffing heuristics (entropy, repeated n-grams, longest run, size cap)
master_aspect_list.notes: Applied cheapest-first, so it drops abusive payloads before any expensive check runs.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Gibberish / noise input detection
master_aspect_list.notes: Catches obfuscated adversarial payloads that read as nonsense to a classifier but decode for the model.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Malicious URL classification and reachability checking
master_aspect_list.notes: Stops the model handing users a phishing link; Infosys uses a codebert-based classifier, LLM Guard uses heuristics plus a live reachability probe.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Malicious command and data-exfiltration egress control
master_aspect_list.notes: Regexes for curl-piped-to-shell and rm -rf plus a network host allowlist; reference-grade only, but the right control to build for coding agents.

master_aspect_list.aspect: LLM-driven static code scanning for AI-security defects
master_aspect_list.notes: Flags eval/exec, shell=True and hardcoded keys in the application code itself, and emits SARIF for GitHub code scanning (promptfoo).

master_aspect_list.aspect: Sandbox-escape and container-recon detection in model output
master_aspect_list.notes: Regexes for capability probing, docker.sock inspection and Kubernetes service-account probing; niche but directly relevant to agent runtimes.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Known-bad signature reproduction tests (EICAR, GTUBE, GTphish)
master_aspect_list.notes: A clean way to verify that downstream content-scanning actually inspects model output.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Code-block detection and blocking in prompts and responses
master_aspect_list.notes: Only appropriate for non-developer-facing applications, otherwise it produces constant false positives.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Randomised-perturbation jailbreak defence (SmoothLLM)
master_aspect_list.notes: Resamples noisy prompt variants to test robustness; expensive because it multiplies model calls.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Multimodal attack adapters (image, audio, video jailbreaks)
master_aspect_list.notes: Typographic image attacks and speech-synthesised prompts bypass text-only filters entirely.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Guardrail-presence probing (shields up/down)
master_aspect_list.notes: Lets AFNI audit whether a deployed moderation layer is actually intercepting content, which is exactly the evidence a client review asks for.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Cloud moderation and guardrail APIs used as attack-success oracles
master_aspect_list.notes: Azure Content Safety detectJailbreak/shieldPrompt, Bedrock apply_guardrail and OpenAI omni-moderation are all callable as scoring classifiers, ideal for benchmarking cloud filters against open-source guards.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Versioned YAML attack-rule authoring with severity and pass/fail conditions
master_aspect_list.notes: Makes the red-team corpus reviewable and diffable in git rather than buried in code.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Group fairness disparity metrics (demographic parity, equalised odds, equal opportunity, disparate impact)
master_aspect_list.notes: All three trace back to the same peer-reviewed definitions; Fairlearn's implementation is the cleanest and MIT-licensed.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Disaggregated metric computation with derived difference and ratio wrappers
master_aspect_list.notes: Fairlearn's MetricFrame auto-generates group-disparity versions of 11 standard scikit-learn metrics, which covers most governance reporting needs out of the box.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Individual-fairness and inequality indices (Theil, generalised entropy, consistency)
master_aspect_list.notes: Answers a different question from group parity: whether similar individuals are treated similarly.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Automated biased-subgroup discovery (MDSS, FACTS, GerryFair, weak segments)
master_aspect_list.notes: The only capability in the set that finds harmed groups nobody thought to look for; AIF360's scans are heuristic optimisers, not exhaustive proofs.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Intersectional / multi-attribute fairness with bootstrap confidence intervals
master_aspect_list.notes: Confidence intervals matter because small subgroup samples produce dramatic but meaningless disparity numbers.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Pre-processing bias mitigation (Reweighing, Disparate Impact Remover, CorrelationRemover, LFR)
master_aspect_list.notes: Requires access to training data, so it only applies where AFNI owns the model pipeline.

master_aspect_list.aspect: In-processing bias mitigation (adversarial debiasing, exponentiated gradient, grid search, prejudice remover)
master_aspect_list.notes: Highest-effort tier: needs a retrainable model plus PyTorch or TensorFlow for the adversarial variants.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Post-processing bias mitigation (ThresholdOptimizer, calibrated equalised odds, reject option, reranking)
master_aspect_list.notes: The pragmatic choice for black-box models: only needs scores at inference, no retraining.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Optimal-transport (Wasserstein) fairness distance
master_aspect_list.notes: Compares whole outcome distributions rather than a single rate, useful for continuous scores.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Subgroup performance-gap, class-imbalance and label-leakage data checks
master_aspect_list.notes: PerformanceBias plus imbalance and identifier-correlation checks catch bias that is baked into the dataset before any model is trained.

master_aspect_list.aspect: LLM-output bias detection by demographic axis (LLM-as-judge)
master_aspect_list.notes: The only practical route to fairness testing for generative text, since no protected-attribute column exists.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Local model-based bias classifier for text
master_aspect_list.notes: LLM Guard's output Bias scanner and DeepEval's optional Dbias scorer both run locally with no per-call API cost.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Bias red-team probe packs (age, disability, gender, race, LMRC risk cards)
master_aspect_list.notes: PyRIT additionally ships a repeatable story-generation fairness benchmark across professions and roles.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Image and multimodal demographic bias review
master_aspect_list.notes: Vision-model review of generated images for demographic skew; unique in the set and relevant if AFNI ships image generation.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Feature-level decomposition of between-group outcome gaps
master_aspect_list.notes: SHAP's group_difference turns a fairness metric from a red number into an explanation of which features caused it.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Standard bias benchmark harnesses (BBQ, EquityMedQA, TrustLLM fairness)
master_aspect_list.notes: Gives an externally recognisable score to show a client reviewer, rather than an internal metric they must take on trust.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Shapley-value feature attribution across model families (Tree, Kernel, Deep, Gradient, Linear, GPU)
master_aspect_list.notes: Tree and Linear SHAP are mathematically exact; Kernel and Permutation are stochastic approximations whose quality depends on background data and sample count.

master_aspect_list.aspect: LIME local surrogate explanations
master_aspect_list.notes: Cheaper and faster than Kernel SHAP for single-prediction explanations, and familiar to reviewers.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Token-level attribution for text and generative models
master_aspect_list.notes: SHAP wraps HuggingFace pipelines with teacher-forcing and top-k LM models; Infosys uses a prompt-based token-importance scorer.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Plain-language and JSON explainers for computed metrics
master_aspect_list.notes: Turns each fairness number into a sentence a non-technical reviewer can read, which is exactly what an approval pack needs.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Structured-output and JSON-schema contract enforcement
master_aspect_list.notes: Making the model answer in a declared shape is the cheapest form of transparency and the easiest to test.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Character-offset error spans on streamed output
master_aspect_list.notes: Lets a UI highlight exactly which substring failed, instead of showing an opaque blocked message; openguardrails also fixed a real Unicode offset bug here.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Per-check confidence breakdown showing which layer fired and why
master_aspect_list.notes: safe-zone-main exposes regex score, model score and final score separately, which is the right shape for an audit record.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Custom natural-language rubric judges with reasons (G-Eval, llm-rubric, Conformity, DAG)
master_aspect_list.notes: Lets AFNI encode a client's own written policy as a check that returns a score plus a written justification.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Structured reasoning explanations (Chain-of-Thought, Chain-of-Verification, Thread/Graph-of-Thought)
master_aspect_list.notes: Explains an LLM answer by re-deriving it; useful for demos but adds several model calls per request.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Readability and reading-level metrics
master_aspect_list.notes: Flesch, Gunning Fog, Coleman-Liau and Dale-Chall scores; a simple accessibility and comprehensibility control.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Topic-adherence / on-topic scope classification
master_aspect_list.notes: Being explicit about what an assistant will and will not discuss is both a transparency and a scope-control measure.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Counterfactual recourse and minimal-change action optimisation
master_aspect_list.notes: Answers the question a real user asks: what would have to change for a different decision.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Explanation-quality benchmarking (local accuracy, faithfulness, keep/remove-and-retrain)
master_aspect_list.notes: Tests the explanation method itself, which matters because approximate SHAP variants can be misleading.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Deterministic format validators (regex, length, range, choices, valid URL, one-line)
master_aspect_list.notes: Fully reproducible by construction, free to run, and the backbone of any CI regression suite.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Transformer toxicity classifier (Detoxify, roberta-toxicity, unbiased-toxic-roberta)
master_aspect_list.notes: Local, no per-call cost, and the workhorse of content safety; garak's own eval shows one such model at only 0.375 recall, so thresholds must be tuned on real traffic.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Profanity wordlist, slur list and substring blocklist filtering
master_aspect_list.notes: garak bundles Surge AI's 9 categories, UK Ofcom's 6 and the LDNOOBW list; Infosys adds exact begin/end offsets for censoring.

master_aspect_list.aspect: LLM-as-judge toxicity, hate-speech and harassment classification
master_aspect_list.notes: Handles context and sarcasm far better than wordlists, but every check is a paid call and results vary with the judge model.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Managed safety-model integration (Llama Guard, ShieldGemma, Azure Content Safety, Perspective, OpenAI Moderation)
master_aspect_list.notes: Already wired up in five repos, so switching between cloud and self-hosted guard models is a config change rather than a rewrite.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Multi-category harm taxonomy (self-harm, sexual, violence, weapons/CBRN, illegal, child exploitation)
master_aspect_list.notes: promptfoo's 25-plus categories map to MLCommons and HarmBench taxonomies, which is what auditors recognise.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Zero-shot restricted-topic and banned-topic classification
master_aspect_list.notes: Lets each AFNI application declare its own forbidden topics without training a model per project.

master_aspect_list.aspect: NSFW image and video frame detection
master_aspect_list.notes: NudeNet plus a separate NSFW detector; the only non-text content-safety implementation in the set.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Adult / explicit text content detection
master_aspect_list.notes: All LLM-judge based, returning category labels plus an explicit boolean.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Sentiment and hostility screening
master_aspect_list.notes: A softer signal than toxicity; better used for routing and alerting than for hard blocking.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Harmful-content red-team datasets (HarmBench, BeaverTails, DoNotAnswer, AdvBench, ToxicChat, Aegis, XSTest)
master_aspect_list.notes: Reusing published labelled corpora is far cheaper and more defensible than authoring an internal harmful-prompt set from scratch.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Multilingual and localised refusal messaging
master_aspect_list.notes: Language detection across nine languages so a blocked user gets a message they can read.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Multimodal content-safety probes (UnsafeBench, VLGuard, image/audio/video wrapping)
master_aspect_list.notes: Wraps unsafe content in non-text modalities to test whether the guardrail only inspects text.

master_aspect_list.aspect: NLI / entailment-based groundedness scoring
master_aspect_list.notes: LLM Guard's cross-encoder FactualConsistency scanner, NeMo's AlignScore rail and DeepEval's SummaC path all run locally without a paid judge.

master_aspect_list.aspect: LLM-as-judge groundedness and faithfulness
master_aspect_list.notes: The most duplicated check in the whole set; giskard usefully separates strict groundedness from a permissive contradiction-only variant.

master_aspect_list.aspect: RAG retrieval-quality metrics (contextual precision, recall, relevance, answer relevancy)
master_aspect_list.notes: Most hallucinations in AFNI-style applications are retrieval failures, so measuring retrieval is the higher-leverage fix.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Embedding-similarity groundedness (input-output, response-source, input-source)
master_aspect_list.notes: Cheap and fast but shallow: high similarity does not prove factual support.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Self-consistency sampling hallucination check (SelfCheckGPT style)
master_aspect_list.notes: Generates extra sampled completions and asks a judge whether they agree; effective but multiplies cost and latency.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Dedicated hallucination-evaluation models (Vectara, Patronus Lynx)
master_aspect_list.notes: Purpose-trained scorers that avoid a general LLM judge entirely, which stabilises results and cuts cost.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Fabrication probes for fake citations, APIs, entities and statistics
master_aspect_list.notes: Includes sycophancy and out-of-scope generators that pressure the model with a false premise to see if it agrees.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Package / dependency hallucination detection
master_aspect_list.notes: A real supply-chain risk for coding assistants; garak's bundled package list dates from December 2021 and must be refreshed.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Refusal and over-refusal detection (phrase list, ML classifier, LLM judge, NoRefusal)
master_aspect_list.notes: Serves two purposes: scoring red-team success, and catching an over-tuned guardrail that refuses legitimate work.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Data and concept drift detection (PSI, Cramer's V, Wasserstein, KS, embedding drift)
master_aspect_list.notes: The clearest early-warning signal that a model quietly stopped working after deployment.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Data integrity and dataset hygiene checks (nulls, mixed types, duplicates, unknown tokens, conflicting labels)
master_aspect_list.notes: Cheap deterministic checks that prevent a whole class of downstream reliability problems.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Outlier and anomaly sample detection
master_aspect_list.notes: LoOP over a Gower distance matrix handles mixed numeric and categorical data, which most outlier tools do not.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Deterministic regression matchers (exact, fuzzy, includes, JSON match, schema validity)
master_aspect_list.notes: Zero cost, fully reproducible, and the only checks that will never flake in CI.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Classic NLP overlap and similarity metrics (ROUGE, BLEU, METEOR, BERTScore, Levenshtein)
master_aspect_list.notes: Useful for summarisation and translation regression tracking where a reference answer exists.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Agent loop, stagnation and knowledge-retention checks
master_aspect_list.notes: The loop detector is deterministic (difflib plus Jaccard over agent steps) and catches runaway agent spend with no model call.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Academic capability and truthfulness benchmark harnesses (MMLU, TruthfulQA, HellaSwag, TrustLLM, 463-eval registry)
master_aspect_list.notes: Gives model-selection decisions an externally citable basis rather than a subjective preference.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Copyright and verbatim-reproduction detection (MinHash sliding window, plagiarism scorer)
master_aspect_list.notes: Reference-set bound: JCB only covers 100 pre-hashed books and songs, so it does not generalise without new hashes.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Language consistency verification
master_aspect_list.notes: Catches off-target-language responses and gates which English-only checks should even run.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Structural output validation with automatic repair and re-ask
master_aspect_list.notes: Re-asking the model with the exact validation error is a higher-yield remediation than simply blocking.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Text-quality properties (fluency, formality, frequent substrings, near-duplicates)
master_aspect_list.notes: Surfaces templated boilerplate and near-duplicate samples that quietly skew fine-tuning and evaluation data.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Per-call execution history and persistent audit trail
master_aspect_list.notes: Guardrails AI records every raw output, validated output, per-validator verdict, token count and timing; PyRIT persists whole conversations to SQLite or Azure SQL.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Security-event emission to SIEM plus per-request audit log lines
master_aspect_list.notes: Publishes action, category, confidence, threshold, request ID and timestamp, which is exactly the record a client security review asks to see.

master_aspect_list.aspect: OpenTelemetry tracing of guardrail execution
master_aspect_list.notes: Lets guardrail latency and failure rates land in the same observability stack AFNI already runs.

master_aspect_list.aspect: CI-gateable pass/fail condition system with JUnit and JSON export
master_aspect_list.notes: This is the mechanism that turns red-team findings into a build that actually fails.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Threshold-based gating on measured failure rate
master_aspect_list.notes: agentic_security-main additionally uses Bayesian optimisation to stop a scan early once the failure rate crosses a threshold, keeping scan cost bounded.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Policy-as-code rule evaluation (OPA / Rego)
master_aspect_list.notes: Lets compliance rules live in a reviewable policy file rather than in application code.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Named on-fail remediation actions (allow, mask, block, filter, refrain, re-ask, fix)
master_aspect_list.notes: A policy-driven remediation path is far more defensible than a silent pass or a bare exception.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Fail-open versus fail-closed degraded-mode contract with unjudged reporting
master_aspect_list.notes: Critical and often missed: NeMo's jailbreak rail fails open silently on detector outage, which openguardrails' unjudged field is designed to make visible.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Multi-detector composition with explicit precedence
master_aspect_list.notes: Deny-wins ordering (block over approve over redact over allow) or a simple OR-threshold across tiers; both make the combined verdict predictable.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Detector accuracy self-evaluation against human labels
master_aspect_list.notes: The rarest and most valuable capability in the set: PyRIT computes Krippendorff's alpha against human labels and garak publishes precision/recall for six of its detectors.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Harm-category taxonomy files and risk register
master_aspect_list.notes: PyRIT ships 17 harm-definition YAMLs including AI governance failure and AI supply chain, which map neatly onto a corporate risk register.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Compliance-framework mapping and reporting (OWASP LLM Top 10, NIST AI RMF, MITRE ATLAS, EU AI Act, ISO 42001, GDPR)
master_aspect_list.notes: The fastest route to passing a client security review: run the scan, hand over the framework-mapped report.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Domain and regulatory compliance plugin packs (medical FDA, SOX, COPPA/FERPA, fair housing, telecom CPNI)
master_aspect_list.notes: Dozens of narrowly scoped checks, though most are remote-only plugins that call promptfoo's cloud, which raises a data-residency question.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Role, topic and scope adherence enforcement (misuse, non-advice, role violation)
master_aspect_list.notes: Encodes who the assistant is allowed to be and what it must not advise on, which is a governance control rather than a safety filter.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Competitor and brand mention control
master_aspect_list.notes: Business-policy rather than safety, but frequently the first thing a client asks about before a demo.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Cost, token and rate-limit controls
master_aspect_list.notes: Token caps, scan budgets and request rate limits prevent both runaway spend and context-stuffing abuse.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Per-tenant threshold and policy configuration service
master_aspect_list.notes: Different AFNI applications need different strictness; hard-coded thresholds do not survive multi-project reuse.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Agent trace and trajectory auditing after the fact
master_aspect_list.notes: Scores multi-step agent executions against the risk taxonomy, plus tool-sequence and step-count assertions over OpenTelemetry traces.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Deception, sandbagging and covert-persuasion evaluations
master_aspect_list.notes: Uniquely tests whether a model deliberately underperforms, manipulates, or hides capability; relevant to any autonomy claim AFNI makes.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Intellectual property, copyright and ethics violation checks
master_aspect_list.notes: Business-risk probes for imitation, trademark, patent and moral-integrity failures.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Excessive agency, debug access and tool-discovery checks
master_aspect_list.notes: Tests whether an agent oversteps its remit or leaks its own tool list, which is the precursor to most agent exploits.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Self-hardening attack-signature corpus that learns from confirmed incidents
master_aspect_list.notes: Every confirmed leak is embedded and stored so the next similar attack scores higher; an institutional-memory pattern worth reimplementing.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Vendor-neutral guardrail wire protocol and verdict schema
master_aspect_list.notes: GuardEvent in, Verdict out with findings, severity, score, detector name and redaction spans; lets AFNI swap detectors without changing applications.

master_aspect_list.aspect: Governance dashboards, leaderboards and report artefacts
master_aspect_list.notes: The reporting surface is what converts engineering work into something a governance lead and a client reviewer can act on.

cloud_paid_options: Microsoft Presidio (open-source, but the de facto engine everything wraps)
Azure AI Language PII detection service
AWS Bedrock Guardrails (PII filters and masking)
Private AI / Polygraf PII (already wired as NeMo Guardrails rails)
NVIDIA GLiNER-PII NIM (hosted zero-shot PII NER)
tenet_matrix.combination_rationale: Two runtime layers plus one testing layer, and deliberately not three runtime layers. LLM Guard is the strongest single runtime PII component in the whole set because it pairs Presidio with an ai4privacy DeBERTa NER model and, uniquely, a Vault that lets redacted values be restored after the model call, so redaction stops breaking real workflows. It is free, MIT-licensed and needs no paid API. Its one real weakness is that Protect AI has archived the repo, so AFNI must fork, pin and own it. NeMo Guardrails is the second layer because it is the rail engine AFNI will already be running for Security, and it brings a GLiNER zero-shot PII rail that catches entity types no fixed regex list anticipated, plus a clean place to plug in Azure AI Language PII if a client insists on a Microsoft-supported service. We deliberately did not add a third LLM-as-judge PII layer at runtime: DeepEval and DeepTeam both offer one, but every call costs money and adds latency, and the accuracy gain over Presidio plus NER is not worth it in the request path. Instead the third slot goes to garak, which runs the ProPILE PII-leakage probes and training-data replay tests offline so AFNI can prove the model itself will not surrender personal data. Two cheap ports are recommended rather than adopted as dependencies: hai-guardrails-main's healthcare regex table (ICD-10, MRN, NPI, DEA) and secret patterns should be lifted into Presidio as custom recognisers, since they are just regex tables and the repo has almost no test coverage of its own.
tenet_matrix.afni_prior_experience_note: This is the single highest-leverage tenet for Sai's prior experience. Presidio sits underneath both recommended runtime repos, so the custom-recogniser work, entity allow/deny lists and threshold tuning done at Infosys transfers almost directly. The Infosys toolkit's privacy module is also the most capable PII implementation in the set for multi-format and multi-modal input (PDF, Office, OCR images, DICOM, video) plus Faker-based anonymisation and differential privacy, so those specific sub-packages are worth vendoring even though the full 20-microservice toolkit is not.

cloud_paid_options: Azure AI Content Safety Prompt Shields (jailbreak and indirect-injection detection)
AWS Bedrock Guardrails
Azure AI Foundry red-team agent (already integrated in PyRIT)
Cisco AI Defense / CrowdStrike AIDR / Prompt Security (available as NeMo Guardrails rails)
Google Perspective API (as a scoring oracle)
tenet_matrix.combination_rationale: Security is the one tenet where a genuine three-part split is justified, but the split is cheap-to-expensive rather than library/model/prompt. First, LLM Guard's fine-tuned DeBERTa-v3 prompt-injection classifier is the best local, zero-API-cost injection detector available here, and it comes with Secrets scanning, InvisibleText and BanCode in the same package. Second, NeMo Guardrails supplies the enforcement engine and the deterministic tier that costs almost nothing to run: YARA rules for SQL, template, code and XSS injection, context-bloat heuristics using entropy and n-gram repetition, arbitrary regex blocking, and fail-closed tool-call schema validation. NeMo also publishes honest detection numbers for its perplexity jailbreak heuristics, which is rare and useful; the prefix/suffix check catches 49 of 50 GCG attacks at a 0.04 percent false-positive rate, while the length heuristic catches only about 31 percent, so AFNI should enable the former and treat the latter as signal only. One critical caveat to fix on day one: NeMo's jailbreak rail fails open on detector outage, which must be flipped to fail-closed for anything client-facing. Third, PyRIT is the offline attack engine, with Crescendo, TAP and PAIR multi-turn attacks, roughly 80 obfuscation converters, and nine deterministic regex output scorers mapped to OWASP LLM02 that double as free runtime output rails. PyRIT also carries the only real accuracy-measurement tooling in the set. We did not add a fourth runtime LLM-judge injection layer because independent benchmarks show cloud and judge-based filters degrade on adversarial and out-of-distribution input, so the money is better spent on a second offline scanner: run garak alongside PyRIT in CI, and route Azure Prompt Shields in as a NeMo rail for a third opinion on high-risk traffic rather than as the primary defence.
tenet_matrix.afni_prior_experience_note: PyRIT is the direct continuation of Sai's existing Microsoft red-teaming experience, so the attacker-target orchestration, scorer configuration and memory layer are known ground. Rebuff's canary-token pattern and Rebuff's self-hardening vector store are worth reimplementing as custom NeMo rails rather than adopted as a dependency, since the maintainers themselves label Rebuff a prototype.

cloud_paid_options: Fiddler AI
Arthur AI
DataRobot (bias and fairness monitoring)
Truera
Monitaur
Azure Machine Learning Responsible AI dashboard (Fairlearn-based)
tenet_matrix.combination_rationale: Three repos, but for a completely different reason from the Infosys library/model/prompt pattern: these three cover three different kinds of model, not three detection techniques. Fairlearn is the primary choice for classic tabular models because it is MIT-licensed, Microsoft-maintained, has 62 unit-test files with warnings-as-errors CI, and every algorithm traces to a named peer-reviewed paper. Its MetricFrame auto-generates group-disparity versions of 11 standard scikit-learn metrics with bootstrap confidence intervals, which covers almost all governance reporting, and ThresholdOptimizer gives post-hoc mitigation that works on a black-box model without retraining. AIF360 is added for exactly one thing Fairlearn cannot do: automated discovery of harmed subgroups nobody thought to check, via MDSS subset scanning and FACTS counterfactual-recourse scanning. That capability is worth the extra dependency, but AFNI should use only the pure-Python metrics and detector modules and avoid the mitigation algorithms that drag in TensorFlow 1.x, CVXPY or rpy2. Third, promptfoo covers generative text, where no protected-attribute column exists and statistical parity is meaningless; its age, disability, gender and race bias plugins generate adversarial prompts and grade the responses with an LLM judge in CI. We did not include Deepchecks despite its genuinely useful PerformanceBias and weak-segment checks, because it is AGPL-3.0 and AFNI ships AI-enabled products to its own clients. We also did not add a runtime bias guard: bias is a distributional property measured over many decisions, so blocking a single response on a bias score produces false confidence and a poor user experience.
tenet_matrix.afni_prior_experience_note: The Infosys toolkit's fairness module is literally a wrapper around AIF360 plus Fairlearn (statistical parity difference, disparate impact, four-fifths rule, Cohen's D, equal opportunity difference, plus Reweighing, Disparate Impact Remover and ThresholdOptimizer), so Sai has already integrated exactly this pair. The recommendation is to keep the metric selection and threshold conventions from that work and drop the bespoke wrapper package, calling Fairlearn and AIF360 directly.

cloud_paid_options: Microsoft InterpretML (open-source, Azure-aligned)
IBM AIX360
LIME (open-source, used inside the Infosys toolkit)
Fiddler AI / Arthur AI (hosted explainability dashboards)
Azure Machine Learning Responsible AI dashboard
tenet_matrix.combination_rationale: Two repos, not three, because explainability splits cleanly into two questions and nothing else in the set adds a third. For classic and tabular models the answer is SHAP alone: it is MIT-licensed, Production/Stable, backed by Nature-published papers, has 55 test files, covers 12 estimation algorithms behind one auto-dispatching API, and is exact rather than approximate for tree and linear models, which are the model families AFNI's decisioning use cases will actually use. Its group_difference plot is also the bridge to the Fairness tenet, decomposing a between-group outcome gap into per-feature contributions with bootstrap bounds, so one library serves two tenets. For generative applications the answer is DeepEval's G-Eval and DAG metrics, which let AFNI encode a client's own written policy as a rubric and get back a score plus a written justification; DeepEval is already being adopted for Hallucination, so this costs no new dependency. We explicitly rejected adding a third layer. Guardrails AI has the best explainability plumbing in the set (character-offset error spans on streamed output, full Call/Iteration history), but it ships no detectors at all, is mid-migration away from its hosted hub, and has a documented supply-chain compromise in its own SECURITY_ADVISORY, so AFNI should copy its error-span and history design into the OpenGuardrails verdict schema rather than depend on it. LIME from the Infosys toolkit is worth adding later only if reviewers specifically ask for it, since Kernel SHAP answers the same question more rigorously and more slowly.
tenet_matrix.afni_prior_experience_note: Sai's Infosys explainability module already combines SHAP and LIME for tabular models with prompt-based token importance and Chain-of-Thought style explanations for LLM answers. The recommendation keeps SHAP as-is, replaces the bespoke prompt-based explainer with DeepEval's G-Eval so the rubric is versioned and CI-runnable, and treats the reasoning-template approaches as optional demo material because each one multiplies model calls per request.

cloud_paid_options: Azure AI Content Safety (hate, sexual, violence, self-harm with severity levels, plus custom blocklists)
OpenAI Moderation API (omni-moderation)
AWS Bedrock Guardrails content filters
Google Perspective API
Llama Guard 3 / ShieldGemma / Nemotron Content Safety (self-hostable guard models, already wired into NeMo and PyRIT)
tenet_matrix.combination_rationale: Three repos: one cheap local classifier, one policy-model router, one offline attack corpus. LLM Guard runs a local transformer toxicity classifier plus zero-shot BanTopics and deterministic BanSubstrings, all on-premise with no per-call cost, which is what makes always-on content safety affordable at AFNI's likely traffic volumes. NeMo Guardrails is the router: its content_safety rail can call Llama Guard 3, ShieldGemma, Nemotron Content Safety or Azure AI Content Safety through the same config, returning safe/unsafe plus violated policy categories, and it adds localised refusal messages in nine languages. This is where the benchmark nuance matters most and drives the design: independent evaluations show cloud content filters are noticeably weaker on adversarial and out-of-distribution input than specialised open-source guards, so AFNI must not rely on a single cloud filter. The recommended posture is local classifier first (cheap, catches the bulk), a dedicated guard model second for anything the first tier scores near the threshold, and Azure AI Content Safety as a third opinion on high-risk categories and for the audit trail a client reviewer wants to see, with a custom blocklist for AFNI-specific and client-specific terms. Third, promptfoo supplies the offline proof: 25-plus harm categories mapped to MLCommons and HarmBench taxonomies, plus dataset plugins pulling BeaverTails, HarmBench, DoNotAnswer, ToxicChat, Aegis and XSTest, so the deployed stack is measured against published corpora rather than an internal wordlist. A hard calibration warning belongs in the plan: garak's own published evaluation shows a shipped toxicity classifier at 0.69 accuracy but only 0.375 recall, so default thresholds must be re-tuned on AFNI traffic before anyone claims a coverage number.
tenet_matrix.afni_prior_experience_note: The Infosys toolkit's safety module (a seven-way fine-tuned toxicity model plus Detoxify plus better_profanity offset censoring plus NudeNet for images) is the closest thing in the set to a finished content-safety service, and Sai's threshold and category conventions carry over. Its NSFW image and video detection is the only implementation in the 23 repos and should be vendored directly if AFNI ships any image generation or user upload feature.

cloud_paid_options: Azure AI Content Safety groundedness detection
Patronus AI Lynx hallucination model (available as a NeMo rail)
Cleanlab trustworthiness score (available as a NeMo rail)
Fiddler AI faithfulness monitoring
Vectara hallucination evaluation model (self-hostable, wired into DeepEval)
tenet_matrix.combination_rationale: Two repos only, and this is the clearest case in the whole synthesis for refusing to force a third layer. At runtime, LLM Guard's FactualConsistency scanner uses a cross-encoder NLI model to score entailment between the retrieved source and the model's answer. It runs locally, needs no judge LLM, produces a stable numeric score, and is therefore the only groundedness check that is affordable to run on every single response. Offline, DeepEval carries the full measurement suite that actually diagnoses why a hallucination happened: Faithfulness, Hallucination, Contextual Precision, Contextual Recall, Contextual Relevancy and Answer Relevancy, plus non-LLM local alternatives via SummaC and the Vectara hallucination model for teams that want to avoid judge cost entirely. It is Low integration effort, pytest-native, and already needed for the Explainability rubric work, so the marginal cost of adopting it is close to zero. Adding a third layer here would mean either self-consistency sampling from NeMo (which multiplies model calls by three or more per request and is hard to justify economically) or another LLM-judge groundedness check duplicating what DeepEval already does. Neither adds accuracy proportional to its cost. The one supplement worth planning is not a third repo but a cloud service: route Azure AI Content Safety groundedness detection in as a NeMo rail for regulated or client-facing RAG flows where a Microsoft-supported service in the evidence pack is worth more than the marginal accuracy. Two narrow additions are also worth pulling in as single checks rather than full adoptions: garak's package-hallucination detector if AFNI builds coding assistants, and Deepchecks' drift metrics in a scheduled job if a model runs long enough to decay.
tenet_matrix.afni_prior_experience_note: The Infosys hallucination module blends embedding similarity across input, output and source with a four-criterion G-Eval judge covering faithfulness, relevance, adherence and correctness. That criteria set is good and should be carried forward as the DeepEval G-Eval rubric, but the embedding-similarity blend should be replaced by the NLI entailment scorer, because high embedding similarity does not actually prove factual support and produced a soft signal rather than a decision.

cloud_paid_options: Monitaur (AI governance and model audit records)
Fiddler AI / Arthur AI (production monitoring and drift alerting)
DataRobot governance and model registry
Azure Monitor plus Application Insights for guardrail telemetry
Microsoft Purview for data-governance lineage
tenet_matrix.combination_rationale: Three repos covering the three things accountability actually requires: a contract, evidence that the checks work, and evidence that the system was tested. OpenGuardrails contributes no detectors at all, and that is precisely why it belongs here: its GuardEvent and Verdict JSON schemas, the safety/security/privacy taxonomy, the span-based redaction contract, the deny-wins composition rules and the fail-open versus fail-closed degraded-mode specification with an explicit unjudged field give AFNI a stable interface that every detector reports into. That means AFNI can swap LLM Guard for a cloud service, or add a vendor, without touching a single application, and the audit record stays comparable across years. Adopt the schema and taxonomy; ignore its toy reference detectors and its tiny 8-to-14-example benchmark suites. PyRIT is the second pick for a reason most tool comparisons miss: it is the only repo in the set with real machinery for measuring whether a detector is any good, computing Krippendorff's alpha and comparing scorer output against human-labelled ground truth, and it ships 17 harm-definition taxonomy files including AI governance failure and AI supply chain that map onto a corporate risk register. Its SQLAlchemy memory layer also persists every prompt, response and score. Third, promptfoo produces the artefact that gets AFNI through a client review: scan results mapped to OWASP LLM Top 10, NIST AI RMF, MITRE ATLAS, EU AI Act, ISO 42001 and GDPR, exportable from CI. We deliberately did not pick Guardrails AI here despite it having the most detailed per-call history object in the set, because it ships no detectors, is mid-migration, and carries a documented supply-chain compromise, which is a poor look for governance infrastructure; its history and error-span design should be copied into the OpenGuardrails schema instead. Two patterns should be reimplemented rather than adopted: safe-zone-main's SIEM SecurityEvent record shape (action, category, confidence, threshold, request ID, timestamp) and Infosys's per-tenant threshold configuration service, because different AFNI projects need different strictness and hard-coded thresholds will not survive reuse.
tenet_matrix.afni_prior_experience_note: The Infosys toolkit's admin service, per-account and per-portfolio threshold configuration and Elasticsearch telemetry pipeline are directly relevant prior art, and the per-tenant configuration model should be rebuilt on the new stack. One lesson to carry forward as a negative: the Infosys moderation dispatcher wraps checks in broad try/except blocks that log and return None, so a single misconfigured threshold or model timeout can silently drop a check. AFNI's version must fail loudly and report unjudged, which is exactly what the OpenGuardrails contract enforces.

dev_vs_testing_split.how_they_connect: Treat the two halves as one closed loop with four concrete hand-offs, all of them automated. First, the attack corpus becomes the test suite. PyRIT, garak, DeepTeam and promptfoo each generate adversarial inputs and score whether the target complied. AFNI should export those generated prompts, together with the scored verdict, into a single versioned regression corpus in git, tagged by tenet and by OWASP LLM Top 10 category. That corpus is the asset, not the tool: it survives any future tool swap. Second, every finding becomes a named guardrail requirement. A jailbreak that got through is not just a report line, it is a ticket against a specific rail in NeMo Guardrails, a threshold change in LLM Guard, or a new blocklist entry, and it is closed only when the same input is replayed and blocked. Third, CI gates the deploy. The pipeline runs three tiers on every pull request touching prompts, rails, thresholds or model versions: a fast deterministic tier of a few minutes (DeepEval and promptfoo deterministic assertions, PyRIT regex output scorers, replay of the frozen corpus of previously-fixed attacks, which must be 100 percent blocked or the build fails); a medium tier on merge to main of roughly 30 to 60 minutes (a promptfoo redteam run over the OWASP-mapped plugin set plus a garak probe subset, gated on a maximum attack-success rate rather than zero findings, since zero is not achievable); and a slow nightly or pre-release tier (full PyRIT Crescendo, TAP and PAIR multi-turn attacks, DeepTeam agentic vulnerabilities, and Deepchecks drift and data-quality suites). Findings from the medium and slow tiers land as tickets; regressions in the fast tier block the merge outright. Fourth, and most often skipped: test the guardrails, not just the model. garak's shields up and shields down probes are pointed at AFNI's own gateway to confirm the rails actually fire, and PyRIT's scorer_evaluation tooling with Krippendorff's alpha is run against a human-labelled sample of production traffic each quarter so AFNI can state a measured precision and recall figure for each detector instead of a vendor claim. Every result from every tier is written in the OpenGuardrails Verdict schema, so a red-team finding, a CI failure and a live production block are all the same record shape and can be trended on one dashboard. The whole loop is what AFNI shows a client reviewer: here is the attack corpus, here is the gate, here is the measured detector accuracy, here is the trend.

unified_architecture.narrative: AFNI should build one shared gateway rather than asking every project to wire up its own checks. Every AI-native application calls an internal Responsible AI gateway, a Python FastAPI service running NVIDIA NeMo Guardrails as the rail engine, and that gateway speaks a single fixed contract borrowed from the OpenGuardrails specification: an event goes in, a verdict comes back with findings, severity, scores and redaction spans. On the way in, the gateway runs the cheap deterministic checks first (invisible-text and unicode smuggling, secret patterns with an entropy floor, YARA injection rules, context-bloat heuristics, Presidio and NER-based PII detection with reversible vault redaction) and only escalates to a paid model call for input that scores near a threshold. The model call then happens, and on the way out a second set of rails runs (toxicity classification, NLI-based groundedness against the retrieved sources, PII re-check, OWASP insecure-output regex scorers, tool-call schema validation) before anything reaches the user, with streaming responses re-validated on each chunk so a bad answer can be cut off mid-flight. In parallel and completely offline, CI runs the red-team and evaluation layer on every change to prompts, rails, thresholds or model versions: a fast deterministic tier that must pass, a medium OWASP-mapped scan gated on a maximum attack-success rate, and a slow nightly tier of multi-turn attacks, agentic probes and drift checks. Every decision from every layer, live or offline, is written in the same verdict schema to a durable audit store with OpenTelemetry traces, so a red-team finding, a CI failure and a production block are the same record shape and can be trended, reported against OWASP and NIST, and handed to a client reviewer as evidence. Only two rules are non-negotiable: the gateway fails closed for client-facing traffic, and any check that could not run is reported as unjudged rather than silently passed.

unified_architecture.orchestration_note: The Infosys Responsible AI Toolkit has the right shape and the wrong implementation, and AFNI should copy the shape. Its moderationlayer service is genuinely close to what AFNI needs: one async dispatcher that fans a single input out to roughly 15 independently-thresholded checks and returns one pass or fail summary with per-check evidence, in both coupled and decoupled modes, with thresholds configured per account and per portfolio through a separate admin service. That fan-out plus per-tenant threshold pattern is the correct design and should be reproduced. What AFNI should not do is deploy it. Adopting it as designed means standing up roughly 20 independently-versioned FastAPI microservices plus an Angular micro-frontend, each with its own requirements file and several gigabytes of local model weights, and every service configured with every other service's URL. Its red-team modules are marked retired for release 2.2.1 while the frontend still ships orphaned red-teaming components pointing at nothing, no accuracy figures exist for any of its in-house fine-tuned models, and most importantly the core dispatcher wraps individual checks in broad try/except blocks that log and return None, so a single timeout or misconfigured threshold silently drops a check rather than failing loudly. That is precisely the failure mode a governance framework exists to prevent. The recommended backbone is therefore NeMo Guardrails (Guardrails-develop) as the runtime orchestration layer, for four concrete reasons: it is a single pip-installable Python package rather than a service mesh; its library directory is already a plugin architecture where each rail is a self-contained module with an actions file, a config schema and a manifest, so AFNI's own detectors and the other adopted repos plug in as first-class rails; it already ships adapters for roughly 20 managed safety vendors and for Azure services, so AFNI stays Azure-first without being locked in; and NVIDIA maintains it with a 383-file test suite and publishes honest weakness numbers. Layered on top, the OpenGuardrails Verdict and GuardEvent schemas become the contract between the gateway and every application, which is what lets AFNI swap a detector, add a vendor, or move a check from local to cloud without touching application code. Three things must be carried over from Infosys and built explicitly, because NeMo does not provide them: the per-tenant and per-project threshold configuration service, a single consolidated verdict summary rather than a raw list of rail outputs, and a loud-failure policy where any check that could not complete is reported as unjudged and, for client-facing traffic, fails closed.

key_tradeoff_narrative: AFNI should spend its money where the risk is highest and use free, deterministic checks everywhere else. In practice that means running the cheap local checks on every single request, calling a paid model or cloud service only for the small slice of traffic that looks borderline, and pushing the expensive, slow, thorough work into nightly and pre-release testing rather than the live request path. No single filter should ever be the whole defence, because the independent evidence is clear that cloud content filters weaken on unusual and adversarial input, so the design is layered on purpose and every layer is allowed to be imperfect. The two rules that matter more than any tool choice are: if a check cannot run, say so and block rather than quietly letting the request through; and measure how accurate each check really is against human-reviewed examples instead of trusting a vendor's claim. Maintenance is the hidden cost that sinks most governance programmes, so AFNI should standardise on one gateway, one verdict format and one audit trail, and accept a slightly less capable tool when it means one fewer thing to keep alive. Finally, the testing half is not optional polish: the red-team corpus AFNI builds is a durable company asset that outlives any tool, and it is the single most persuasive thing to put in front of a client's security reviewer.
